label: Chapter 6 · Part A
title: The Nature of God I: Background Principles & the First Attributes
tagline: From “there is a First Cause” to “here is what it must be like”
oneSentence: Armed with three general principles — proportionate causality, “action follows being,” and the analogy of being — we can deduce from the conclusions of the five proofs that the First Cause is one, absolutely simple, unchanging, immaterial, timelessly eternal, and necessary, and that each proof reaches the very same God.
bigPicture:
Chapters 1–5 each ended with a cause of the world: a purely actual actualizer, an absolutely simple One, a divine intellect holding the abstract objects, subsistent existence itself, and a necessary being. A skeptic can fairly ask two things at this point: *why think these are one being rather than five?* and *why call any of them “God”?* This chapter answers both. It first lays out the general tools of reasoning that let us move from the world, considered as an effect, to the nature of its cause, and then it derives, one by one, the classical divine attributes.

The tools come first because the rest depends on them. The **principle of proportionate causality** (PPC) says a cause cannot give what it does not in some way have. **Agere sequitur esse** (“action follows being”) says what a thing does cannot outrun what it is. The **analogy of being** explains how words like “exists,” “power,” or “knows” can be applied literally to God without making him just a bigger version of us (univocal predication) and without emptying the words of all meaning (equivocal predication). Feser defends each principle independently of theism, and shows that even naturalist philosophers quietly rely on the first two.

With the tools in hand, Feser derives the first group of attributes: **unity** (there can be only one purely actual being, and the five proofs converge on it), **simplicity** (no parts of any kind — the attribute that anchors all the others and defines classical theism), **immutability**, **immateriality**, **eternity** understood as strict timelessness, and **necessity**. Along the way he answers a whole string of modern critics: Cottingham on proportionate causality; Plantinga, Morris, and the “theistic personalists” on simplicity; Swinburne, Pike, and Kenny on timelessness; Findlay, Russell, and Schrader on necessary being.

This part matters for persuasion as much as for understanding. Many objections to the five proofs (“Why only one God?”, “Isn’t your God just a cosmic superman?”, “Who made God?”, “How can a changeless God act?”) are really objections to the *nature* of the God concluded to. This module shows how tightly the attributes interlock: deny one — especially simplicity — and you lose the First Cause itself. Part B (module ch6b) continues with omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility, and God’s ongoing relation to the world.
objectives: State the principle of proportionate causality, explain the formal/virtual/eminent distinction with the $20 example, and show how PPC follows from the principles of causality and sufficient reason.
Answer Cottingham’s “heirloom,” sponge-cake, triviality, and evolution objections to PPC.
Explain agere sequitur esse, its relation to formal causes, and how naturalists like Churchland and Searle implicitly rely on PPC and this principle.
Distinguish univocal, equivocal, and analogical predication, and within analogy distinguish attribution, proper proportionality, and metaphorical proportionality — with an example of each.
Reconstruct Feser’s seven-step argument that “being” is analogical and explain why confining God-talk to univocal or equivocal terms leads to agnosticism or atheism.
Derive God’s unity from pure actuality and explain why the five proofs must all reach one and the same God.

Explain why divine simplicity is nonnegotiable for classical theism and rebut Plantinga’s and Morris’s objections using the analogy of being, the essence/property/accident distinction, and Cambridge properties.

Derive immutability, immateriality, timeless eternity, and necessity, and answer the objections from acting, life, temporal causation, simultaneity, linguistic conventionalism, and Schrader’s “empty world.”
Identify when an objection commits the fallacy of accident or begs the question against the proofs, and explain why.

summary.heading: Opening: five proofs, one question left
summary.body:
Feser opens with a compact recap. The **Aristotelian proof** reasons from potentials being actualized to a purely actual actualizer. The **Neo-Platonic proof** reasons from composite things to an absolutely simple cause. The **Augustinian proof** reasons from abstract objects (universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds) to a divine intellect in which they exist as ideas. The **Thomistic proof** reasons from the real distinction between essence and existence in things to a cause that is subsistent existence itself. The **rationalist proof** reasons from the principle of sufficient reason to an absolutely necessary being.

So far the focus has been on *that* God exists, with only glimpses of *what* he is and *how* he relates to the world. This chapter takes up those two topics. Because that requires reasoning from the world as effect to God as cause, Feser first sets out several general philosophical principles and only then applies them.

summary.heading: The principle of proportionate causality: formally, virtually, eminently
summary.body:
The PPC, first met in chapter 1, says that whatever is in an effect must be in its **total cause** in some way — because a cause cannot give what it lacks. The key refinement is that the effect’s features may be in the cause in one of three ways. Feser’s illustration: you end up with a $20 bill.

- **Formally**: I hand you a $20 bill from my wallet. I have the very “form” I give you.
- **Virtually**: I have no bill, but I have $20 in the bank and wire it so you can withdraw it. The total cause (me plus my account) contains the effect’s content in another mode.
- **Eminently**: I have neither bill nor funds, but I can get a genuine $20 bill printed on a Federal Reserve press. I have something causally *more* fundamental than a bill — the power to make bills.

PPC is not an arbitrary add-on. It follows from the **principle of causality** (PC) and the **principle of sufficient reason** (PSR), both defended in earlier chapters. An aspect of an effect that came from nothing in its total cause would be a potential actualized by nothing (violating PC) and a feature with no explanation (violating PSR).

summary.heading: Cottingham’s counterexamples and the triviality charge
summary.body:
John Cottingham (criticizing Descartes’ version of the principle) says PPC presupposes an “heirloom” picture in which properties are handed down from cause to effect, and offers counterexamples: helium has properties absent in the hydrogen it fuses from; a sponge cake is spongy though no ingredient — eggs, flour, butter — is spongy.

Feser gives three replies. **First**, the examples consider only the *materials*, while PPC concerns the *total* cause (the baker, the oven’s heat, the chemistry of mixing and baking, and so on). Restricting PPC to material factors and then refuting the restricted version is a straw man. **Second**, the heirloom reading assumes the effect must be in the cause *formally*, which defenders of PPC explicitly deny. A Thomist writer (Coffey) notes that a boy need not have a black eye in order to give one; Aquinas says a hot body does not pass its own numerically identical heat to another but, by its power, actualizes a new heat that was potential in the thing heated. **Third**, Cottingham grants that sponginess doesn’t arise from nothing but says that calling it “potentially” present makes PPC trivial. Feser accepts the word *potentially* — the bank account’s potential to be drawn on, the printing press’s potential to print — but denies triviality: explanation in terms of potentialities may be only *minimally* informative, yet minimal is not the same as empty.

summary.heading: PPC at work outside theology: Churchland, dualism, and evolution
summary.body:
That PPC is substantive shows up in the fact that naturalists use it. Paul Churchland argues that since human beings (individually and as a species) arise from purely material beginnings by purely material processes, the result must be purely material. That inference assumes that a wholly material total cause yields a wholly material effect — PPC. The mind-body dualist accepts the same principle but runs it the other way: since the intellect is not material, the total cause cannot have been wholly material. Both sides take PPC for granted.

Evolution is sometimes offered as a counterexample (simpler forms giving rise to more complex ones). But even on the standard naturalistic account, a simple organism does not just produce a more complex one out of nothing. Existing genetic material, a mutation (from a copying error in DNA replication or from radiation or chemical damage), and environmental conditions *together* produce a new variation — no one of them sufficing alone. That respects PPC. Feser adds the physicist Paul Davies’ point that denying that new biological information derives from some combination of prior factors (including the environment) would conflict with the second law of thermodynamics, according to which order and information tend to decrease in a closed system. Conclusion: PPC is well grounded independently of natural theology, yet highly useful for reasoning from the world to its divine cause.

summary.heading: Agere sequitur esse: action follows being
summary.body:
The Scholastic principle *agere sequitur esse* says that what a thing does reflects what it is. Eyes and ears work differently because they are built differently; plants take in nutrients, grow, and reproduce while stones do none of these, because plants are alive and stones are not. Feser presents the principle as the counterpart, for **formal causes**, of what PPC says about **efficient causes**. An efficient cause brings about a thing’s existence or a change in it, and PPC says the effect cannot exceed that total cause. A formal cause is a thing’s nature — what makes it the kind of thing it is (for a human, rational animality). A thing’s characteristic attributes and activities flow from its nature (language flows from our rationality), and they cannot exceed that nature any more than an effect can exceed its cause. A stone that grew and reproduced would no longer be a stone.

Like PPC, the principle follows from PSR: an activity outrunning its nature would have no explanation. A footnote adds an important qualification: a thing can do what exceeds its nature when *something else* makes it do so, as a puppet’s wooden limbs move when the puppeteer moves them. What is ruled out is a thing doing so *on its own*.

summary.heading: Agere sequitur esse among naturalists: Aquinas, Searle, and property dualism
summary.body:
Aquinas’ best-known use of the principle is his argument for the soul’s survival: intellectual activity is (on independent grounds) immaterial; a material thing cannot carry out an immaterial activity; so the soul is immaterial, and since immaterial things lack the natural tendency to decay that material things have, the soul does not perish with the body. A materialist will reject the premise that thought is immaterial, but can still accept the conditional: *if* intellectual activity were immaterial, its subject would have to be immaterial too.

In fact the naturalist John Searle argues along exactly these lines against **property dualism** (the view that mental properties are immaterial yet are properties of a material brain). Searle’s complaint is that the view is unstable: if a mental property is really something over and above the brain, it isn’t a property of the brain but a separate kind of entity; if it really is a property of the brain, it isn’t over and above it. Other critics find it mysterious how a wholly material brain could produce immaterial properties. Feser does not try to settle that debate; the point is that *agere sequitur esse*, like PPC, is not a Scholastic relic but something many secular philosophers are implicitly committed to.

summary.heading: The analogy of being: univocal, equivocal, analogical
summary.body:
Recalling chapter 2, Feser distinguishes three uses of terms. **Univocal**: “Fido is a dog,” “Rover is a dog” — the same sense. **Equivocal**: a “bat” flying in the attic and the “bat” you swing — unrelated senses. **Analogical**: “this wine is good,” “George is a good man” — not the same sense, but not unrelated either.

Talk of *being* or *reality* is analogical. A stone and its color and shape are all real, but not in the same way: the color and shape exist only *in* the stone, modifying and depending on it, while the stone doesn’t exist in another thing that way. Yet it isn’t that the stone is real and its attributes unreal (the way a baseball bat is simply not a flying mammal). So being is said of substance and attribute neither univocally nor equivocally, but analogically.

summary.heading: Kinds of analogy: attribution and proportionality
summary.body:
Feser distinguishes two main types of analogy.

**Analogy of attribution.** “George is healthy,” “this is healthy food,” “George’s complexion is healthy.” George is the **primary analogate**; the food and the complexion are **secondary analogates**. Health exists intrinsically only in George; the others are called healthy only because of their relation to him — the food as a *cause* of health, the complexion as an *effect and sign* of it.

**Analogy of proportionality**, which divides into two:

- **Proper proportionality**: “life” said of plants, animals, humans, and angels. Here the feature exists *intrinsically* in each analogate (unlike attribution) and *formally* in each — each really has the nature of being alive, though in very different ways.
- **Improper (metaphorical) proportionality**: “that is a lion” (at the zoo) versus “George is a lion.” Something intrinsic to George (his courage) grounds the usage, but the form of lionhood is literally present only in the animal.

Metaphor is one kind of analogy, but not all analogy is metaphor. And it is the analogy of proper — that is, nonmetaphorical — proportionality that is crucial for the concept of being.

summary.heading: Why “being” is not a genus; proportional similarity
summary.body:
“Being” applies to substances, to attributes, to things whose essence and existence are distinct, and to that whose essence just is its existence — by an analogy of proper proportionality. The concept is applied to each in an indistinct, indeterminate way, on the basis of a real likeness among them, rather than in exactly the same way.

This differs from a univocal term applied to very diverse things. “Animal” applies to fish, birds, and reptiles in exactly the same way, naming a **genus**; what distinguishes them is their **specific difference**, which lies outside the genus (you can grasp rationality without grasping animality, or atomic number 79 without grasping metal). But being is not a genus. You cannot grasp substance or attribute *without* grasping them as beings, so their differences are not extrinsic to being. Indeed, the only thing outside being is nonbeing, and nothing cannot differentiate anything.

Instead, being is predicated by **proportional similarity**. Compare “I see the tree” and “I see that the Pythagorean theorem is true.” The seeing is radically different in the two cases, but eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem; that similarity of *relations* grounds using the one concept. In the same way, a man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s existence is to its essence as God’s existence is to his essence — though the relation differs in each case (in God existence is *identical* to essence; in an angel it actualizes the potential essence of a wholly immaterial being; in a man it actualizes the essence of something with material and immaterial operations). A footnote adds that being is *also* predicated by analogy of attribution, with God, whose essence is existence, as the primary analogate and creatures as secondary analogates insofar as he causes them to exist.

summary.heading: The argument that being is analogical
summary.body:
Feser grounds the analogy of being in the act/potency distinction, which change forces on us (chapter 1). His seven-step argument, paraphrased: actuality is real; potentiality is real; they are really distinct; if potentiality were real in the same (univocal) sense as actuality, they would not be distinct; if it were real only in an equivocal sense, it would not be real at all; the three uses exhaust literal usage; so potentiality is real in a sense analogous to actuality’s.

He defends each premise. Denying premise 2 is **Parmenides’** denial of change, already shown incoherent. Denying premise 1 is the extreme **Heraclitean** view (on a traditional reading) that only change is real, with nothing stable. That is equally incoherent: there would be no persisting self to move from premises to conclusion, no single stable argument to repeat to critics or to oneself; change always heads *toward* some outcome (a melting ice cube moves toward liquidity and flatness — new actualities); and a thing changes as it does because it is actually a certain kind of thing (it melts because it is water, not wood or glass). Premise 3 holds because the real distinction of essence and existence (chapter 4) is already a case of real potency/act distinction, and because calling the distinction merely conceptual would amount to saying only one of the two is real — denying 1 or 2. Premise 4 holds because sameness of sense would make one a kind of the other; premise 5 because being in a wholly unrelated sense just means being unreal; premise 6 because the three uses exhaust literal predication.

This gives grounds for analogical predication, and for the analogical character of “being” in particular, that are independent of any argument for God — someone could accept act and potency without accepting the Aristotelian proof.

summary.heading: Why this matters for God-talk: between silence and nonsense
summary.body:
The significance for natural theology is enormous. The proofs lead to something radically unlike anything we experience — purely actual, simple, immaterial, immutable, eternal. Words fitted to changeable, composite, material, temporal things cannot apply to such a being univocally; if to be a being *just meant* to be material and changeable, God would not be a being in that sense.

If we had only univocal language, we could say only what God is *not* — a purely **apophatic** or negative theology. But then we could not even say that God *exists* or that he *causes* the world, which are affirmative claims; the negative way is part of the story, not all of it, or it would undercut the very arguments that got us to God. Equivocal language is no escape: if God’s “power” means something wholly unrelated to power, what does it mean? Any attempt to fill in “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___” either uses a univocal term (reviving the first problem) or an equivocal one (compounding the second). Confined to these two options, we would end in agnosticism — or even atheism, if we couldn’t say what “God exists” means. The resolution is the third, independently motivated use: analogical predication — attribution and proper proportionality — lets us speak **literally and positively** about God.

Feser notes (as in chapter 2) that this is not special pleading: physics also stretches ordinary words — entities that are both wave-like and particle-like, *space itself* being curved — and seems intelligible only if understood analogically. We should expect the same when describing a level of reality more fundamental than physics.

summary.heading: Unity, step one: no potentiality even in God’s activity
summary.body:
Feser now turns to the attributes, starting with **unity**: there is, and in principle could be, only one God. Chapter 1 showed that things mixing act and potency depend at every moment on something purely actual. A critic might grant that the First Cause’s *existence* involves no actualization while suggesting that its *activity* (such as actualizing other things) does.

Feser gives two replies. **First, agere sequitur esse**: if a thing exists in a purely actual way, how could it act in a less than purely actual way? Existence is what is most fundamental in a thing; where in its nature would these less fundamental potentials for activity come from? **Second, composition**: a being with actual existence but potential activity would have parts — an actual part and a potential part. As chapter 2 showed, a composite needs a cause that unites its parts, and that cause must be extrinsic (an intrinsic one would be self-causing, which is incoherent). This holds even if the thing always existed: the question is why the parts are combined *at all*, which calls for an *ontologically* prior cause even if there is no *temporally* prior one. But a First Cause with a cause is not the first cause and cannot end the hierarchical regress. So God is purely actual, without qualification.

summary.heading: Unity, step two: why there can be only one purely actual being
summary.body:
For there to be more than one thing of a kind, there must be a distinction between an individual and its species, or (for a species) between the species and its genus — and any such distinction brings with it a distinction between potentiality and actuality.

Take the human species, with the essence *rational animal*. Animality and rationality are distinct metaphysical parts of that essence: rationality is one way of being an animal, not the only way, so it must be *added* to animality. Being an individual human adds a further part — the matter of one’s body, which distinguishes one human from another. Each part brings potentiality: the matter is potentially a human or some other kind of thing, and must be actualized as a human; the genus animal is, of itself, potentially rational or nonrational. Anything with parts of any kind is a mixture of act and potency, since parts only potentially compose a whole until actualized — even if the actualization never had a temporal beginning. (A footnote closes a loophole: one cannot distinguish two purely actual beings by other sorts of parts, such as substance and accidents, since *any* composition entails potentiality.)

So multiplicity within a kind requires composition, composition requires potentiality, and God has no potentiality. God is therefore not a member of a kind that could have other members: he is unique, and the theism the proofs reach is monotheism.

summary.heading: One God, five paths
summary.body:
Feser then shows that the five proofs reach the same God by showing that their key descriptions are mutually entailing.

- **Pure actuality ⇔ absolute simplicity.** Whatever has parts mixes act and potency, so the purely actual is simple. Conversely, something simple must be actual (or it would not exist) and can have no potentiality (or it would have an actual part and a potential part). So the Unmoved Mover of chapter 1 is the One of chapter 2.
- **Pure actuality ⇔ subsistent existence.** Essence and existence, where distinct, are related as potency to act, so the purely actual cannot have an essence distinct from its existence. Conversely, what just *is* subsistent existence cannot depend on some potential being actualized, or its existence would be derived, making it one more dependent thing. So chapter 1’s cause is chapter 4’s.
- **Simplicity ⇔ subsistent existence**, directly: a simple thing cannot have an essence distinct from its existence (that would be a metaphysical part), and subsistent existence can have no parts of any other kind either (parts entail potentiality).
- **All of these ⇔ absolute necessity.** A contingent being would need some potential actualized and would have parts (at least essence plus existence) needing combination; conversely, a necessary being can have neither potentiality nor parts, or its existence would depend on them.

So the necessary being of chapter 5 and the necessarily existing intellect of chapter 3 are the same as the purely actual actualizer, the One, and subsistent existence itself. These are not five deities but five routes to one God.

summary.heading: Simplicity: the heart of classical theism
summary.body:
Feser stresses that unity cannot be separated from **simplicity**. If God contained a genus/difference or essence/existence distinction, there could in principle be more than one God. His status as First Cause also depends on it: any parts at all — act and potency, essence and existence, or others — would mean he needs a cause like everything else.

So to deny divine simplicity is implicitly to deny God’s uniqueness and ultimacy. Making God an instance of a genus turns him into a member of a pantheon, *even if the sole member* — Zeus and Odin would have the same nature even if they were the only residents of Olympus and Asgard. Making him something that needs a cause reduces him to a creature, even if the one creature that happens to lack a cause (and allowing an uncaused composite would undercut the proofs themselves). Insisting that he is immaterial doesn’t help: that yields a kind of superangel, and worshiping it would be idolatry. Denying that anything is simple amounts to atheism.

Hence the mainstream of Western philosophical theology — pagans (Aristotle, Plotinus), Jews (Maimonides), Muslims (Avicenna, Averroes), Christians (Athanasius, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas) — treated simplicity as nonnegotiable. The Catholic Church taught it at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and the First Vatican Council (1869–1870); Luther and Calvin affirmed it. It is the core of **classical theism**.

summary.heading: Theistic personalism and Plantinga’s critique
summary.body:
Recently some theistic thinkers have rejected simplicity. They have been dubbed “neo-theists” (Norman Geisler) and “theistic personalists” (Brian Davies, who lists Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, and Charles Hartshorne). The label reflects their treating God as the unique member of a species under the genus *person*, alongside humans and angels, but without their limits. The dispute is *not* about whether God is personal — classical theists ascribe intellect and will to God — but about whether being personal puts God in a genus and makes him composite. (Some, like process theologian Hartshorne, even say God changes — which already implies potentiality and composition.)

**Plantinga** argues that simplicity says God is identical with each of his properties, so all his properties are one, contradicting the obvious fact that God has several (power, mercy), and makes God a property and hence an abstract object. Feser replies that Plantinga reads the doctrine through three assumptions of his own: (1) a very broad sense of “property” covering anything predicable (being human, wise, barefoot, married to Xanthippe, Plato’s teacher, even being Socrates and one’s essence); (2) properties as Platonic abstract objects in a “third realm”; (3) univocal predication.

Classical theists reject all three. (a) **Analogy**: power and knowledge are distinct *in us*, but what we call power and knowledge in God are only analogous to ours, so their distinctness needn’t carry over. Plantinga also misreads analogy as nonliteral — but attribution and proper proportionality are literal: nonunivocal does not mean nonliteral. And no classical theist says God is a “property” to begin with; that is Plantinga’s straw man. (b) **Metaphysics of essence**: we must distinguish a thing’s **essence** (rational animality), its **properties** in the strict sense that flow from the essence (the capacity to be amused), its **contingent accidents** (skin color — still intrinsic), and mere **relations** (being Plato’s teacher). And these are concrete constituents of the thing, not Platonic Forms it participates in — what Nicholas Wolterstorff calls a “constituent ontology.” The odd results — that creating humans would be as essential to God as wisdom, that God is an abstract object — come from Plantinga’s assumptions, not from the doctrine. When Plantinga replies that the word “property” doesn’t matter since these are all “characteristics,” he misses that Aquinas’ point is metaphysical, not verbal.

Plantinga also misses what is at stake. The worry isn’t just Platonic participation but **causal dependence** and **uniqueness**. Human rationality and animality can exist apart, so something must combine them; if God’s wisdom and power were distinct, something would have to combine *them*. A God who participates in a divine essence or belongs to a genus would be unique only as a matter of contingent fact. Such a being would be a quasi-divine ersatz, powerful but essentially creaturely — and nothing in the proofs supports even that, since each concludes to a wholly noncomposite cause. Classical theism and simplicity stand or fall together; denying simplicity is implicitly atheism; the proofs show atheism false; so simplicity is true.

summary.heading: Morris’s objection and Cambridge properties
summary.body:
Thomas Morris (following a line also in Christopher Hughes) argues that God has some things true of him necessarily (omnipotence) and some only contingently (having created the world — he could have refrained), so he must have both necessary and contingent properties, which cannot all be identical.

Setting aside the loose use of “property,” Feser draws on Barry Miller, who builds on Peter Geach’s distinction between **real** properties and mere **“Cambridge” properties** (named for Cambridge philosophers like Russell and McTaggart who used the notion). If Socrates grows hair, that is a real change in him. If Socrates becomes shorter than Plato only because Plato grew, Socrates has undergone a mere Cambridge change and acquired a Cambridge property. Simplicity rules out God’s having contingent *real* properties, not contingent Cambridge ones; and it says his *real* properties are identical, not all his properties. Being Creator is a Cambridge property: it involves the world coming to be, not a change in God. So omnipotence (real, necessary) and being Creator (Cambridge, contingent) are indeed not identical — but simplicity never said they were. A footnote anticipates the rejoinder that creating is like Socrates *causing* Plato to change, which does involve change in Socrates; that assumes the changes agents like us undergo must belong to every agent — a fallacy of accident, taken up next.

summary.heading: Immutability
summary.body:
Change is the actualization of potential; God has no potential to actualize; so God cannot change. Doesn’t creating involve a transition from not creating to creating? No: becoming Creator is a Cambridge change, like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato — the real change is in the world, not in God. Immutability means no *real* change in God, not no Cambridge change. Immutability also follows from simplicity: a real change is a change in one respect while remaining the same in others (a substance loses an attribute while keeping its identity and other attributes), which requires parts. A simple being has none.

**Objection: acting requires changing.** When I type, not only the screen changes; my fingers, nervous system, and thoughts change too. Feser replies that inferring that *every possible* agent must change in acting commits the **fallacy of accident** — like inferring that any possible professor must be under nine feet tall because every actual one has been. Following Brian Davies: what is essential to acting is producing an effect in another, not changing oneself; what is essential to teaching is causing someone to learn, not lecturing or writing books specifically. What is essential to creating is simply causing the world to exist.

**Objection: a changeless God couldn’t be alive.** Same fallacy. On the Aristotelian account, life is operating from an **internal principle** (immanent causation) rather than being wholly moved from outside (transient causation, as when a thrown stone breaks a window). God acts without being acted upon at all — unlike living things that must eat and breathe — so he has life in the fullest possible way.

summary.heading: Immateriality and incorporeality
summary.body:
That God has no body and is wholly immaterial follows at once from pure actuality and simplicity, on either of two views of matter.

**Aristotelian view**: every material object is a composite of **substantial form** and **prime matter**, and matter just is the potentiality to take on form — prime matter by itself is pure potentiality. A simple being lacks the composition; a purely actual being lacks the potentiality.

**Any view**: material things have parts — the visible ones (the wood, plastic, or metal of furniture, an animal’s organs) and the microscopic ones (molecules, atoms, subatomic particles), which can be arranged and rearranged, implying potentiality. Even fundamental particles (fermions and bosons), though not made of smaller particles, have distinct attributes — parts in a broad sense — and they come into being and pass away. So nothing material can be purely actual and simple.

summary.heading: Eternity: no beginning, no end — and no time
summary.body:
God neither comes into being nor passes away. Whatever begins has parts needing combination — above all essence and existence — is merely potential until combined, exists contingently, and so needs a cause. God has no parts, no potentiality, exists necessarily, and just is existence; so he not only needs no cause but *could not* have one. Likewise, whatever ends has separable parts (its essence can come apart from existence), is potentially nonexistent, and is contingent; God, being existence itself, can hardly lose existence. What neither begins nor ends is eternal.

But divine eternity is not mere **longevity** (existing through all past and future time); it is **strict timelessness**. This follows from immutability: a God in time would keep adding days and years to his life, would act differently at different moments, and (since he has knowledge — argued in Part B) would keep learning new facts like “it is now t1,” then “it is now t2.” All that is change. It also follows from simplicity: a temporal life has distinct stages, i.e., parts. Feser notes that William Lane Craig, who rejects both immutability and timelessness, agrees that an immutable God would be timeless.

summary.heading: Two objections to timelessness
summary.body:
**Temporal causing.** Feser has argued that God causes the existence of things at every moment. If God causes something to exist at t1 and at t2, doesn’t he act at t1 and then again at t2 — and so exist in time (Swinburne, Pike)? No. Following Davies, from *God causes it to be the case that X exists at t1* it does not follow that *at t1 God causes X to exist*. God does not perform a string of successive acts — creating at t1, conserving at t2, conserving again at t3. From outside time, in a single act, he causes a temporal world in which the object exists at t1, t2, t3, and so on. Compare (with Stephen Barr) an author who conceives a whole story in one flash of insight: for the characters, the middle comes after the beginning, but the author didn’t devise the beginning first and the ending later.

**Simultaneity.** If Socrates’ existence in 469 B.C. is simultaneous with God’s eternity, and Obama’s existence in A.D. 1961 is too, then by the transitivity of simultaneity Socrates and Obama would be simultaneous — absurd (Swinburne, Kenny). Feser (citing Davies and Paul Helm) replies that this treats eternity as a *point in time*, since only a point in time can be simultaneous with another. The whole claim is that God is not at any point in time but outside time altogether.

summary.heading: Necessity: the conventionalist objection
summary.body:
The rationalist proof argues directly for a necessary being, and the other proofs imply it. Some reject the very idea. J. N. Findlay (and Bertrand Russell, in his 1948 BBC debate with Frederick Copleston) held that necessity is purely a matter of linguistic convention: “all bachelors are unmarried” is necessary only because it is analytic — true by the meanings of words — and tells us nothing about reality. Extralinguistic reality can’t be necessary; God would be part of extralinguistic reality; so a “necessary being” makes no sense.

Feser replies in two ways. **First**, conventionalism fails on independent grounds. It confuses **sentences** (linguistic items) with **propositions** (not linguistic). “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition, which would be true even if no language had ever existed. So the conventionality of sentences doesn’t make propositions or their necessity conventional. That example is contingent, but mathematical and logical truths — 2 + 2 = 4, everything is identical to itself — are necessary and notoriously hard to treat as mere conventions (see chapter 3). **Second, and deeper**, the objection begs the question. The proofs claim to show there is an extralinguistic, necessarily existing cause, and they give an account of that necessity with nothing to do with language: pure actuality, absolute simplicity, identity of essence and existence. Simply asserting that all necessity is conventional presupposes the arguments are wrong without showing it.

summary.heading: Necessity: Schrader’s empty world
summary.body:
David Schrader argues that we can imagine a world containing only a single green marble, and then imagine even the marble gone — a world with nothing at all, not even God. So God doesn’t exist in every possible world and is not necessary.

**First reply**: this works only if everything that exists or could exist, God included, is the sort of thing one can form a **mental image** of. It isn’t. Picture “2 + 2 = 4” chalked on a board as the only existing thing, then picture it erased; that does nothing to show 2 + 2 = 4 is not necessary, because numbers aren’t imageable objects. You can picture numerals (“2,” “4,” or Roman “II,” “IV”), but numerals are labels, not numbers. What we can picture is irrelevant to what we can strictly conceive. The same goes for God, who is not material: you can’t picture God existing, let alone not existing (Feser cites Brian Leftow).

**Second reply**: even setting imagery aside, the method of settling necessity by consulting what we can conceive in possible worlds — common in contemporary philosophy — gets things backward from the Aristotelian-Thomistic point of view. We start from *actual* things, discover their essences, and from there infer what is possible or necessary for them. In God’s case: first establish that he exists, then determine his nature (purely actual, simple, subsistent existence depending on nothing), and from that infer that he exists necessarily — and so, if we use possible-worlds talk, in every possible world. That is exactly what the previous chapters did. Schrader’s objection doesn’t refute this; it assumes it is wrong, and so begs the question. With necessity established, the chapter turns to omnipotence (covered in Part B).
